title: Hedwig (16 October)
hook: a duchess walks barefoot through the snow, carrying the shoes she was told to wear

segments.voice: Yesterday, Callistus, the slave who became bishop of Rome and welcomed sinners back. Your line was from slave to shepherd. Whose second chance did you notice? Day one thousand thirty-six.

Winter in Silesia. A duchess is walking to church barefoot, on frozen ground, as she does to share a little of what the poor feel. Her confessor, worried, orders her to wear shoes. She obeys. She carries them. That's the story people tell, and it's half a joke and half a portrait: a woman who did what she was told, and still found a way to stand where the poor stood. Today, Hedwig.
screen: `BAREFOOT ON FROZEN GROUND.` → `TOLD TO WEAR SHOES.` → `SHE CARRIES THEM.`

segments.voice: Hedwig was born into a noble family in Bavaria and married Henry, who became duke of Silesia, a land now mostly in Poland. So she was German by birth and Silesian by marriage, and today both Germans and Poles honor her. In Polish, she's Jadwiga. She had wealth and power, and she spent a great deal of both on others. With her husband she founded a convent at Trzebnica for Cistercian nuns, and she supported hospitals and fed the poor, tradition says, sometimes serving them at her own table. Her life was not easy. She outlived her husband and some of her children. Her son Henry was killed in battle defending the land against invaders. In her last years Hedwig lived at the convent she had founded, among the nuns, and she died there. What made her giving different? It wasn't only large gifts from a distance. It was close: walking where the poor walked, eating with them, using her rank to open doors for them. Paul has a line about that kind of giving, in the Douay-Rheims: "For God loveth a cheerful giver." The Greek word behind cheerful there is hilaros: glad. A glad heart, not a grim duty. And it doesn't take a duchy. In the same verse Paul says each one should give as he has decided in his heart, and a chapter earlier he says a gift is measured by what a person has, not by what he hasn't. Out of what you have. Hedwig had a great deal and gave it gladly. The same gladness fits a smaller purse.
screen: `GERMAN BY BIRTH, SILESIAN BY MARRIAGE.` · `A CONVENT, HOSPITALS, BREAD FOR THE POOR.` · `LAST YEARS IN THE CONVENT SHE FOUNDED.` · `GOD LOVETH A CHEERFUL GIVER.` · then, large: `OUT OF WHAT YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give from what you have. Settle and breathe. Take a quiet inventory: not your money only, but your time this week, a skill, a coat you don't wear, a meal you could share. Let one thing rise to the top, something you could actually give. Notice whether the thought of giving it feels glad or grim. If you pray, you can offer it to God and ask for a cheerful heart. If you don't, simply decide when you'll give it. The bell holds the time.
Hedwig. Jadwiga in Polish. A duchess of Silesia who founded a convent, fed the poor, walked where they walked, and gave gladly.
Your line: the duchess who gave. Today, give the one thing you chose, and give it with a glad face. Day one thousand thirty-six.

howItsDone: Saint Hedwig is remembered on 16 October; she is honored in Poland and Germany, and Catholics in Silesia, especially at Trzebnica where she is buried, keep her feast with Mass and pilgrimage.

myth: Hedwig of Silesia is the same saint as Queen Jadwiga of Poland
they're two different women; Hedwig was a duchess of Silesia.
she was born in Bavaria and became duchess of Silesia by marriage.
the shoe story says she refused to obey her confessor
in the story she obeyed; she just carried the shoes.

fork.setup: you're Hedwig. your confessor orders you to stop walking barefoot in winter and wear shoes. what do you do?
options: ignore him and keep walking barefoot
put the shoes on and stop worrying
carry the shoes in your hands
fork.reveal: the story people tell says she obeyed the order to have shoes, and carried them.

original.note: the Greek word Paul uses for a cheerful giver in 2 Corinthians 9:7: glad, joyful.

trapdoor: what you thought: a medieval noblewoman with a famous name.
what it means: a duchess who gave her wealth and her presence to the poor, gladly.
what a scholar hears: Germans and Poles both claim her; she is sometimes confused with Queen Jadwiga of Poland, a different saint.

sources.quoted: For God loveth a cheerful giver.

notes: Born in Bavaria (Andechs), duchess of Silesia, founder of Trzebnica for Cistercian nuns, son Henry II killed fighting the Mongols at Legnica, retirement to Trzebnica: confirm details as written.
'She outlived her husband and some of her children': confirm.
The barefoot-and-shoes story is told as a story people tell; confirm.
Greek hilaros (ἱλαρός) behind 'cheerful' in 2 Cor 9:7: confirm form (the verse has ἱλαρὸν).
'Silesia, a land now mostly in Poland': confirm wording.
'Paul says each one should give as he has decided in his heart' paraphrases the first half of 2 Cor 9:7.

Editor: fixed the order of events (Hedwig lived at Trzebnica after her husband's death in 1238, before her son Henry fell in 1241, so 'after that grief she withdrew' was wrong; now 'in her last years'), with the matching screen head; 'out of what you have' is now attributed to 2 Corinthians 8:12, paraphrased and cited, instead of being folded into 9:7; trapdoor 'often confused' softened to 'sometimes'.
Audit: facts, dates (Henry I d. 1238, Henry II at Legnica 1241) and 2 Cor 9:7 / 8:12 re-checked; no repetition of days 1017-1035 found; no changes.
